H1.text: Usually, we get an equation and find its roots.

H2.text: Ravi turned it around for Aarav. I am thinking of a quadratic. Its roots are two and five. What is my equation?

H3.text: Aarav had it on his study table in ten seconds.

H4.text: Then Ravi pushed harder. Roots one plus two i and one minus two i. Can you still build it, with no i in the equation?

H5.text: Yes. Today we build quadratic equations backwards, from their roots.

P1.text: Start with the simplest idea. A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero.

P2.text: So x minus two, times x minus five, equals zero, is true when x is two, and when x is five. Nowhere else.

P3.text: Multiply it out. x squared minus seven x plus ten equals zero. That is Ravi's equation.

L1.text: Now let the roots move, and watch the equation rebuild itself. The roots stay equally far from three.

L2.text: Roots one and five. Their sum is six, their product is five. The equation is x squared minus six x plus five.

L3.text: Slide them together. The sum stays six, the product grows.

L4.text: Roots three and three. The product is nine. x squared minus six x plus nine, which is x minus three, squared.

L5.text: Now step off the number line. Three plus i and three minus i. The product is nine plus one, which is ten.

L6.text: At three plus two i and three minus two i, the product is thirteen. The equation is x squared minus six x plus thirteen, with no i in sight.

L7.text: Quick one. The roots are four and minus one. What is the constant term? Pause and think.

L8.text: Minus four! The constant is the product of the roots, and four times minus one is minus four. The equation is x squared minus three x minus four.

R1.text: Now the general rule, in small steps. Call the roots alpha and beta.

R2.text: Step one. x minus alpha, times x minus beta, equals zero. It is zero exactly at alpha and at beta.

R3.text: Step two. Multiply out. x squared, minus alpha x, minus beta x, plus alpha beta.

R4.text: Step three. Group the middle terms. x squared minus alpha plus beta, times x, plus alpha beta, equals zero.

R5.text: Step four. In words: x squared, minus the sum times x, plus the product, equals zero.

R6.text: This is the last episode, run backwards: with a equal to one, the middle coefficient is minus the sum.

S1.text: But is it the only equation with those roots? Side by side.

S2.text: x squared minus seven x plus ten. Its curve crosses the axis at two and five.

S3.text: Two x squared minus fourteen x plus twenty. Every coefficient is doubled. The curve is steeper, but it crosses at the same two points.

S4.text: So any non zero number k times the equation has the same roots. That is why we say a quadratic, not the quadratic.

K1.text: Your turn. Does minus x squared plus seven x minus ten equal zero have roots two and five? Pause and decide.

K2.text: Yes! It is minus one times Ravi's equation. The curve flips, but still crosses at two and five.

T1.text: Remember this. x squared, minus the sum times x, plus the product, equals zero.

W1.text: Now, Ravi's second challenge as a worked example.

W2.text: Form a quadratic with real coefficients whose roots are one plus two i and one minus two i.

W3.text: Step one. The sum is one plus two i plus one minus two i. The imaginary parts cancel, so the sum is two.

W4.text: Step two. The product is one squared minus two i, squared. That is one minus four i squared, which is one plus four. Five.

W5.text: Step three. Put them in. x squared minus two x plus five equals zero.

W6.text: Every coefficient is real. A conjugate pair always gives a real sum and product.

X2.text: Roots two and five. Many students write x squared plus seven x plus ten: the wrong sign in the middle.

X3.text: Its roots are minus two and minus five. The middle term is minus the sum. The right answer is x squared minus seven x plus ten. Always check with a root.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In JEE Main: build a new equation from the roots of an old one, as in April twenty twenty four. It is not in the current NCERT text.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Alpha and beta are the roots of this equation. Which equation has the roots alpha squared and beta squared? Pause and solve.

A2.text: For the old equation, alpha plus beta is three and alpha beta is one.

A3.text: New sum. Alpha squared plus beta squared is the sum squared, minus two alpha beta. Nine minus two, which is seven.

A4.text: New product. Alpha squared beta squared is alpha beta, squared: one. So the equation is x squared minus seven x plus one.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Form a quadratic whose roots are three and minus four.

Y3.text: Two. Why does a conjugate pair always give real coefficients?

Y4.text: Three. Write two different quadratics whose roots are both minus two.
